chunks: When an I2C bus needs multiple controllers. The question: When would you need more masters?
Most I2C buses have one controller, the chip that starts every transfer. But I2C is designed so that two or more controllers can share a bus.
That helps when two processors both need the same sensors.
If two start at the same moment, the bus settles who goes first by itself, with no damage and no lost data for the winner.
Imagine two people starting to talk at once in a meeting. Each speaks one word at a time and listens while doing so.
If you meant to stay silent for a word but hear someone else speaking, you know they are saying something different. You stop and wait, and the other person is never disturbed.
In I2C, speaking is pulling the wire low, and staying silent is letting it go. Speaking always wins.
Two controllers start together and send the first address bits 1, 0, 1, .. (A) and 1, 0, 0, .. (B). The first two bits match, so neither notices anything.
In the third bit A releases SDA (1) while B pulls it low (0). The bus follows B, so at the rising SCL edge A reads 0 where it sent 1: arbitration lost.
From then on A stays off the bus (dashed) while B continues with the bit it was sending, completely undisturbed.
Controller: the chip that starts a transfer and runs the clock. Older documents call it the master.
Arbitration: how two controllers that start together decide who goes on, by comparing what each sends with what the wire shows.
Wired-AND: the wire is low if any chip pulls it low, and high only if all let go. Bus free: the quiet period after a transfer ends with a STOP, when any controller may start.
Sensor hub: a small low-power chip that reads sensors on behalf of a main processor.
Controller A sends the address 0x48 (hexadecimal), which is 1001000 in binary. Controller B sends 0x44, which is 1000100. The first three bits match, so neither notices anything.
On the fourth bit, A releases the wire to send a 1, while B pulls it low to send a 0. The wire reads 0. A sees it sent a 1 but read a 0, so it stops and waits.
B carries on with no damage. The lower address wins. That is the whole idea.
"You need multiple controllers when two devices both need to start transactions on the same bus: a main processor plus a sensor hub, a host and a charger sharing a fuel gauge, redundant controllers.
I2C handles it with arbitration: both drive open-drain lines; whoever releases a 1 but reads back a 0 has lost, stops, and waits for a STOP, while the winner continues uncorrupted.
SCL is wired-AND too, so clocks synchronize. But it adds complexity, so I'd prefer an interrupt line or separate buses when possible."
Quick check. Two I2C controllers start simultaneously. How does a controller detect that it lost arbitration?
